One of my favorite games in the series is FF6, for its story, gameplay, and of course its music. What I love so much about the music in FF6 is how diverse it is. We have the usual awesome battle and character themes, but since the setting of FF6 is akin to 19th century society (as opposed to the medieval settings of previous installments), it is very fitting to include music from what we would consider to be classical eras, and the soundtrack has a lot of similarities to baroque music.

A scene which is both important to the plot and musically significant is the Opera "Maria and Draco." The music was written by Nobuo Uematsu, and the lyrics were written by Yoshinori Kitase. The opera consists of four tracks: "Opening," "Aria di Mezzo Carattere," "The Wedding," and "Grand Finale?". Due to the technical limitations of the SNES, the voices had to be synthesized. Several of the musical themes in the opera can be found in other tracks. The Aria, which is considered one of the most famous musical themes in FF, bears several similarities to Celes' theme, for example.

Opera from OST, see description for timestamps of different movements

Aria cover by Jillian Aversa

Darkness and Starlight by the Black Mages which tries to stay true to the original, with Nobuo in the chorus!

The Impresario from Balance and Ruin (OCRemix), a rock opera that I love which tells an entirely different story from the original

Next I would like to talk about the final boss theme, "Dancing Mad." The theme draws from several themes in the game, including the opening theme and Kefka's theme. It contains four movements and ends with Kefka's laugh. It bears similarities to baroque pieces such as Bach's "Preludes and Fugues" and Handel's "Messiah," the latter being significant due to Kefka being a god at this point in the game. The piece really gives a sense of madness, which is very fitting for Kefka's character. And at almost 18 minutes long, it just keeps going. In Nobuo's words:

Well, usually when you make a song it's two to three minutes in length, you have the introduction, the main part and the ending. But... for 'Dancing Mad' I didn't really put a stop on it, so I kept on working on it, working on it, working on it and that really let the song... you know... I got to play around with it for something like fourteen minutes, and it's really one of my favorites.

Dancing Mad from OST

Orchestral rendition by Distant Worlds

Piano Cover by Hiroyuki Nakayama from the Piano Opera

I apologize for the length of the music this week, but these pieces really do capture the setting so well. Hopefully you enjoy it as much as I do!

Okay so I just wrote a wall of text out and then realised that this is ELI5...

Short version: watch video. Single pendulum: simple motion; we know what it is going to do next. Double pendulum: no idea, have to know everything from before to tell where it's going next. That's why the weatherman is often wrong, he doesn't know everything that came before so he can't see where the weather is going. Chaos theory deals with this weird "random" "unpredictable" motion/systems.

Long version if interested:

Imagine you have a pendulum swinging back and forth. At any time you can calculate its velocity and acceleration based on its position. When the pendulum is at the centre, it is moving fastest, to get to either side. When it is at the side, it stops momentarily to turn around. From this you can calculate where it will be at a given time in the future, and where it was at a given time in the past.

If you attach a second pendulum onto that one, it becomes a double pendulum system, and the second pendulum will pull the first off course, which, in turn, will pull the second one off course, and so on. The result is a bunch of motion that might as well be random. You can't simply take the current position of the pendulum(s) and glean anything from the past or future. I mean sure, you can tell the immediate past and future, but beyond that you really have no idea.

Here is a video illustrating the differences between single and double pendulum systems.

This unpredictable, "random" motion is described as chaotic, and chaos theory is a field of science that deals with it.

A chaotic motion that you will be familiar with from every day life would be the weather. You can't look at the clouds/atmosphere at this moment and discern what it was like before, because it's a bunch of interconnected, interacting systems that all influence each other and all have influenced each other at some point in the past; the number of possible states of the world that could have led to this one is insanely large, and that increases as you look further into the past.

This is why the weather reports have difficulties with accuracy; they do their best to predict the future based on current and past atmospheric conditions and states, but ultimately it is chaotic and we don't have all the data. The solution is to have a perfect simulation of the earth and its atmosphere from its birth to now, and then you can continue the simulation to see what happens in the future, but I don't know how realistic such a thing is, there is just so much that can contribute to and affect the current state it's just ridiculous.

At it's core, the idea is that it's difficult to predict the long-term effects that small changes will have. Here's a real-world example:

  • At university, I signed up for a Philosophy 101 class- which was a likely event, given my interests.

  • I happened to overhear a conversation on gaming, and went over to say Hi. Something I'm not prone to doing.

  • Through networking with one of these guys, I met his roommate.

  • While hanging out with these two, I happened to meet a friend of theirs.

  • This friend went on to become the lead developer and DBA at a defense contractor

  • He then convinced his boss to give me an interview for a BIA job

  • As a result, I got my first "real" job as a software developer.

So, it can accurately be said that much of where I am now can be traced back to a decision to say Hi to a couple of strangers. What would have happened if I hadn't? Don't know, but it would have had some profound effects on my career.
